plan.question: How does a nation confront when its institutions betray justice?

chapters.title: A Nation Divided
beats: In the heart of a proud republic, a single wrongful conviction tore a nation apart. A military court convicted an innocent man of treason, sacrificing truth to preserve institutional honor. The divided France saw its people split into two camps: those who defended the army's honor at any cost, and those who demanded justice even when it meant exposing national shame. As the truth emerged, the conflict revealed deep-seated antisemitism within French society. The case became a test of France's commitment to its own revolutionary ideals. How could a nation founded on equality and justice allow such a miscarriage of justice to persist?

chapters.title: The Players
beats: Paris, France, the center of power and culture, became the battleground for this national crisis. In this city, Captain Alfred Dreyfus, a 35-year-old Jewish officer in the French Army, found himself at the center of a storm. His brother Mathieu would become his chief defender, though he is not among our main players. Opposing Dreyfus stood Major Ferdinand Walsin Esterhazy, the real traitor who had passed French secrets to Germany. Leading the counter-espionage unit was Lieutenant Colonel Georges Picquart, who discovered evidence pointing to Esterhazy. Writer Émile Zola would risk his reputation by defending Dreyfus, while Édouard Drumont, director of the antisemitic newspaper La Libre Parole with circulation of 200,000, fueled the anti-Dreyfusard sentiment. These five men would shape the fate of one innocent man and the soul of a nation.

chapters.title: The Wrongful Conviction
beats: In December 1894, Captain Alfred Dreyfus stood accused of treason, charged with communicating French military secrets to the German Embassy in Paris. Despite the lack of concrete evidence, a military court convicted him based on a single document. The seven judges, influenced by prevailing antisemitism, sentenced the 35-year-old officer to life imprisonment.

Meanwhile, back in Paris, Lieutenant Colonel Georges Picquart had taken over counter-espionage. By 1896, he discovered evidence that identified Ferdinand Walsin Esterhazy as the real culprit. The 'petit bleu' telegram, found by Picquart, revealed Esterhazy's guilt, but the military hierarchy refused to reconsider the case.
chapters.hook: While Dreyfus suffered on Devil's Island, a movement to free him was growing in Paris.

chapters.title: The Turning Point
beats: The truth about Dreyfus's innocence was gaining momentum in Paris. In November 1897, Mathieu Dreyfus filed a complaint against Esterhazy, who was revealed as the author of the bordereau. The following month, Zola published his first article in support of Dreyfus, igniting a firestorm of controversy.

When Esterhazy was brought before a military court in January 1898, he was quickly acquitted, demonstrating the military's commitment to protecting its own. This blatant injustice prompted Zola to take the unprecedented step of publishing 'J'Accuse...!' in the newspaper L'Aurore. In this open letter, Zola directly accused the French government of a major miscarriage of justice and antisemitism.

The publication created a national crisis. The government responded by prosecuting Zola, who faced trial for defamation. The nation watched as this battle played out in court, with intellectuals and ordinary citizens taking sides.

chapters.title: The Reckoning
beats: Zola's prosecution only intensified the public debate. In January 1898, Le Temps published a petition calling for a retrial, signed by prominent figures including Senator Auguste Scheurer-Kestner. The Chamber of Deputies voted to prosecute Zola, who stood trial in April.

Meanwhile, Maurice Barrès lambasted intellectuals in Le Journal, representing the anti-Dreyfusard position. The Supreme Court upheld Zola's appeal, but the military remained steadfast in its position.

The turning point came in July 1898, when Cavaignac reported items 'overwhelming among a thousand' during questioning in the National Assembly. This admission led to the discovery that the color of lines on the 'faux Henry' paper didn't match, exposing the forgery.

In August 1898, Colonel Henry confessed to creating the forgery that had convicted Dreyfus. The next day, he killed himself at Mont-Valérien fortress, a dramatic end to the cover-up. With Henry's confession, the truth could no longer be denied.

chapters.title: Aftermath and Legacy
beats: In 1899, Dreyfus was returned to France for another trial in Rennes. Despite the mounting evidence, the new trial resulted in another conviction, though the sentence was reduced to 10 years. Finally, in 1899, Dreyfus was pardoned and released, though not exonerated.

The truth would eventually prevail. In 1906, Dreyfus was fully exonerated and reinstated as a major in the French Army. During World War I, from 1914-1918, Dreyfus served his country, ending his service with the rank of lieutenant colonel.

In 1935, Dreyfus died in France, having lived to see his name cleared but having spent years fighting for justice. The affair that had divided a nation came to symbolize modern injustice in the Francophone world, remaining one of the most notable examples of a miscarriage of justice and antisemitism. The affair divided France into pro-republican, anticlerical Dreyfusards and pro-army, mostly Catholic anti-Dreyfusards, leaving a permanent mark on French society.
